opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the biggest thing I took away was how *convinced* he is. People know Yann's views from Twitter and talks: LLMs alone won't get us to human-level intelligence, we need systems that understand the physical world, that can predict and plan. But sitting across from him, it wasn't a slogan. He's been thinking about this for decades, and he sees this as the moment where the ideas, the compute, and the data are finally lining up.

What struck me most was his framing that a world model is not a video generator. A lot of people hear "world model" and think of beautiful pixel-perfect videos. His point, which I deeply agree with, is that predicting every pixel is the wrong objective. The world is full of unpredictable details: leaves moving, textures, noise. An intelligent system should learn an abstract representation and predict in that space. That's the JEPA line of thinking, and it's fundamentally about representation learning, which is what I've cared about my whole career.

The second takeaway was about doing this as a company rather than only in academia or a big lab. He was very clear that this needs to be open, research-driven, and patient. It's not "ship a chatbot next quarter." It's closer to building a foundational science bet, and you need people willing to work on problems that might take years to pay off. For me, that was both exciting and a little sobering, because it means you have to protect the research culture while still building something real.

And finally, on a personal level, I came away with this sense that the field is at a fork. The language-model paradigm has been enormously successful, and I don't dismiss it at all. But vision, embodiment, understanding space and physics—these are still wide open. Talking with him made me feel that if there's a time to make a serious bet on that direction, it's now. That was probably the most important thing I walked out with: not a specific plan, but conviction that this is worth doing.

r001.rationale: The response describes building an open, research-driven, patient company, but does not identify the need for a business model as Xie’s takeaway.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the biggest takeaway wasn't about the technology at all. It was about conviction.

Yann has been talking about world models and self-supervised learning for, what, more than a decade now, through periods when almost nobody in the field thought that was the right bet. And when I sat down with him, what struck me was that he didn't frame this as "LLMs are plateauing, so let's try something else." He framed it as, this was always the path, and the field just took a long detour. Whether you agree with him or not, that kind of long-horizon stubbornness is rare, and I think it's actually a prerequisite for building something fundamentally different rather than chasing the current benchmark.

The second thing was a more practical lesson about what a company around this idea would even look like. A lot of people hear "world model" and think it's just a video generator with a nicer name. Yann's view, and mine too, is that generating pixels is not the point. The point is learning representations of how the world works, so that you can predict, plan, and act. That's the JEPA line of thinking: predict in representation space, not in pixel space. If you take that seriously, it changes everything downstream. Your data strategy is different, your evaluation is different, and you can't just borrow the LLM playbook of scaling tokens and hoping intelligence falls out.

And the third thing, which was maybe the most sobering, is that research taste and company building are not the same skill. We talked a lot about how you keep a research culture alive when there's commercial pressure to ship something that looks like a product in six months. Yann's answer was essentially: you have to be willing to say no to the obvious thing. I'm still thinking about whether that's realistic in the current funding environment, where everyone wants a demo yesterday. But I came away feeling that if anyone can hold that line, it's probably him. And I came away with a clearer sense of what I personally find exciting about this direction, which is that for the first time in a while, the "next big thing" in AI is not a foregone conclusion. That's good for research.

r001.rationale: The response discusses what a world-model company might look like and how its data strategy and evaluation would differ, but it does not identify the need for a business model as Xie’s takeaway.

astra-6.text: The way I’d frame it is: a world model is a research direction, but it isn’t yet a company thesis. You still have to explain what capability you’re building, how you’ll know it works, and who needs it. Can the system predict what happens when it takes an action? Can that prediction help it make better decisions? For me, the key question would be how to turn that ambition into something you can test—and then into something useful.

r001.rationale: The response says a research direction is not yet a company thesis and asks who needs the capability, but it does not identify the need for a business model as Xie’s takeaway.
